WORLD OF SPORT.
BILLIARDS.
THE LURE OF THE GREEN

For proof of the growing favour in which billiards is held by all classes, one need only inquire at the nearest library of bookshop. The literature of the game, which those in a position to judge say is enjoying an unprecedented popularity, is probably more considerable than that of any other indoor pastime.

There is undoubtedly a large public for two recently-published technical works, “First Steps to Billards,” by Willie Smith (Mills and Boon, 5s.), and “Advanced Billiards,” by Tom Newman (Long, 21s.), in which the champion probes some of the deeper subtleties of the game. Both books are the outcome of the widespread interest in a game which is no longer regarded as a pastime of profligates, or, at best, as in later Victorian times, a recreation not indulged in by gentlemen.
EARLY PREJUDICE.

That the evolution of billiards has been slower than that of most games may be attributed to the prejudice that periodically has existed against it. The poet Spencer refers to it in unfluttering terms in his "Mother Hubbard's Tale," in which he says of "The Ape":—
A thousand wayes he could them entertain.

With all the thriftless games that may be found:
With mumming and with mask-
ing all around.
With dice, with cards, with balliards, farre unfit.

This antique allusion can appropriately be linked with a�later Spencer, the philosopher, whose opinion of the pastime was adroitly, if possibly unfairly, expressed when to a man who claimed skill at the game, he rejoined that the accomplishment connoted a misspent youth.

FROM "VANITY FAIR."
Thackeray, in "Vanity Fair," points in effect a similar moral in accounting the proficiency of Rawdon Crawley, who, it will be remembered, contrives to live passing well on nothing a year, an economic paradox, partly explained by his dexterity with the cue:

Crawley, from being only a brilliant amateur, had grown to be a consummate master of billiards. Like a great general, his genius used to rise with the danger, and when the luck had been unfavourable to him for a whole game, and the bets were consequently against him, he would, with consummate skill and boldness, make some prodigious hits, which would restore the battle, and come in a victor at the end. Those who were accustomed to it (his play) were cautious how they staked their money against a man of such sudden resources, and brilliant and overpowering skill.

In “The Tour of Dr. Syntax in Search of a Wife,” a questionable impression of the game as it was played at that period is conveyed by the lines that follow those describing how the doctor dined at Tulip Hall with Lady Tulip and the daughters of the family:
At length the temple of perfume Was quitted for the billiard room.
Ladies command, he must obey. So Syntax took a cue to play. Tho' he did not the laugh.
As he proposed to play for love.
Though when the pastime they had done
He was informed, and to his cost The several parties he had lost As they were coolly counted
By the tall Miss. who kept the score.
Whate'er he fancied in their feats.
He could not say he thought them cheats.
ANCIENT ORIGIN.

When it comes to tracing, or attempting to trace, the beginnings of the game, one is faced with much complexity. It is safe to assume that billiards is of considerable antiquity; beyond that, explicitness does not venture. There is pictorial evidence that prototypes of the billiard table we know to-diy were in existence two hundred and fifty years ago. It has been claimed that croquet and billiards have a common ancestor in the game of "paille mille," which was the vogue four hundred years ago.

In or about 1570 a French artist named Devigne drew up rules for a table game in which small bills were knocked through Ironhonn The pastine caught the fancy of Louis XIV, to whose attention it had been commended by the Court physicians, and almost immediately it became fashionable. Soon afterwards "cushions," as we call them, were fixed to the tables, and a third hill was introduced. The balls made of wood or ivory,
were set in motion with the aid of a flat-ended cue, and it was in all likelihood this version of the game that Shakespeare had in mind when, in "Antony and Cleopatra," he prompts Cleopatra to bid Charmian, her maid, "Let us to billiards."

In the latter years of the seventeenth century billiards seems to have risen somewhat in general esteem. Charles Cotton, in the "Complete Gamester," published in 1674, states that there were at that time few towns or great houses that did not possess a public billiard table, for the pursuit of this "most gentle, cleanly, and ingenious game."
$ ^{*} $ ENGLISH IMPROVEMENTS.

Even so, the progress of billiards was singularly slow. It did not become a widely-known game until the end of the eighteenth century, when John Thurston foresaw the possibilities of improved tables and implements.

A cabinet-maker by trade, with premises in Newcastle Street, Strand, Thurston revolutionized the game in a comparatively short time. The wooden bed of the table, the coarse covering, the badly-planned cushions, and the clumsy cues were all abolished in favour of slate slabs, rubber cushions, and pointed cues, and although the game subsequently switchedbacked more than once from vogue to decline, its hold on the imagination of players was never appreciably weakened. Now, without a doubt, the position of billiards among our popular pastimes is as secure as that of any other, and perhaps more so than most.
AUSTRALIA
WOMEN PLAYERS FOR ENGLAND.

Great interest centres round the forthcoming appearances in England of the lawn tennis teeth of Australian women and the part they will play in Home championships. For years we have been accustomed to the doughty deeds of Australian men; the names of Norman Brookes, Jim Anderson, Gerald Patterson, and Patrick O'Elara Wood are blazoned on the records of Wimbledon. In the role of championnis Australian names figure four times, and this year may well add a fifth, for Anderson, now that his visit is kure, is already a strong favourite for the Wimbledon title.

There is every reason, therefore, to anticipate that their women's play will also be of a high calibre. The one qualifying factor is that we know from experience that women players are slower to adapt themselves to strange conditions than men. One remembers the downfall of Mlle. Lenglen and our own women's team in America, and the trials of Mrs. Mallory, Miss Goss, and others on their visits to Europe. But Australians proverbially have a fighting temperment perhaps superior to that of any other tennis-playing nation, are less easily downcast by temporary failure, and so we may expect these characteristics to be shared by their women's team. Between their first three players there is little margin. For Miss Akhurst, the new champion, only just overhauled Miss Boyd in the final after the latter had beaten the reigning champion, Mrs. Harper.

SCHOOLGIRL SPORTS

Both with women athletes and the public relay is now extremely popular. It appeals to the former because it is necessary to those who might have none in individual races. Fluctu is a moderate runner may well be worth her place in a relay team for her skill in the take-over.

Relay races are particularly well suited to schoolgirls because they fast, and develop that "tenan spirit" which, as the Duchess of Atholl, M.P., has told us, is one of sports's most beneficial influences on youth. Therefore relay races are now an established feature of schoolgirl sports, but they are not always conducted on up-to-date lines.
THE PERPETR MPHO.
In many cases the receiver of the baton has to remain on a fixed mark until she has the stick. This means: a standing start. The proper method admits of a flying start, except for the first lap.

James are drawn pulled to the startling line to denote the stations of the second, third and fourth runners. At each station two other lines are drawn ten years, which side of the first, making twenty yards between the nine-and-four boundaries. The two other lines.

'The received wait on or next the back line, watching her partner approach. The new she turns round and starts. It is now for the partner to race up alongside her hard transfer the buton. She may now do so until it is over the first line, while the receiver must have the button in hand when she assesses the far boundary. Otherwise the whole team is disqualified.

When the transfer is skillfully carried out the receiver is well into her stride as she crosses the fine, but it is a difficult operation. In an interview Miss N. E. Callebaat, the one hundred yards champion at the first Women's Olympic and how secretary of the London Olympiad Athletic Club, which held the world's rehearsal record until robbed of it by Gireen Britain at the last international meeting, emphasised the importance of the takeover. "A team of moderate runners," she said, "skilled in it, will always beat a team of champions who bungle the operation." Men usually take the baton with the arm crooked against the side, women with right hand held out behind, thumb and forefinger separated, so that the stick can be thrust into the fork between them. Miss Callebaat thinks the women's method slightly the better, for it saves the giver a step or two.

While writing the receiver should closely wade her partner. If the latter is tiring it is no use running away from her, but if she is finishing strongly the receiver can get going. For this reason a girl who can be trusted to finish strongly is a more valuable member of the team, even if she is on the slow side, than one who dying away to nothing, sweeves or sturnbles as she finishes, perhaps dropping the baton.
CONSTANT PRACTICE

Although the receiver should watch her approaching partner, once she has turned and started she should not again look round. This demands complete confidence between partners, to be attained by constant practice only.
Every effort," said Miss Callebrand, "should be made to establish a lead in the first lap. This should give confidence to the next girl and may dismay her opponent."

Women run 660 yards, divided into laps of 220, 110, 220, 110 yards. Five hundred or 550 yards, suitably divided into laps, should be enough for senior girls, 410 yards for juniors. The longer lap should come first, for the inside position on a round course gives an overwhelming advantage over a short distance. A cool head, steady hand, pluck, and practice with the baton make the successful relay runner.
